e.t: This Hebrew noun means “song.” It refers to sung expression and can function as the object or subject of speech involving singing. The word appears 77 times in the Old Testament corpus, showing its regular use across Israel’s worship, teaching, and musical life. Scripture connects it with speech, musicians, joyful celebration, and worship directed toward God. Its central idea remains a song: something voiced or performed in singing rather than ordinary conversation.

This Hebrew word means “away.” It functions as a predicate, expressing the idea of something being away in relation to another part of the sentence. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Job 27:8. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, its precise force in that sentence cannot be described further; the secure lexical sense is the separation or removal expressed by “away.”

It is used in statements about a subject that comes to perish, so it functions as the action or outcome being spoken of rather than naming a person, place, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Numbers 24:20 and 24:24. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

e.t: Sheleph is a personal name identifying a person in a genealogy. It is rendered as “Sheleph” and appears twice in the Hebrew Old Testament: in Genesis 10:26 and 1 Chronicles 1:20. In both passages, the name is connected with a birth or begetting record, so its function is to identify a named descendant rather than describe an action, quality, or object. The surrounding genealogy supplies the specific family relationships.

e.t: Shimeah is a personal name, referring to a particular man rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears twice, and both occurrences are in 2 Samuel 13. The name identifies the same named person in the surrounding account, where it is used as an object of speech and is associated with discussion of death. Since no broader lexical definition is available, its ordinary meaning here is its function as a personal name: it identifies Shimeah.

e.t: This word refers to Shinar, a place-name in the Hebrew Old Testament. It identifies a geographical region or land rather than describing an action, quality, or person. The name appears eight times across eight Old Testament verses, beginning in Genesis and continuing through Zechariah. Its use in passages connected with major places and kingdoms shows that Shinar functions as a fixed location in the biblical account. The exact significance of the place in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Hebrew word means “basest,” describing someone or something placed at the lowest level of rank or standing. It functions as a descriptive word rather than naming a person, place, or action. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it is recorded once, at Daniel 4:17, so its normal meaning is established from this single occurrence and its rendering. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain its precise force in that passage.

This Hebrew word means “middle,” referring to a central position between or among other parts. It can describe something located at the center of a structure, area, or arrangement. The word occurs 11 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, in passages concerning structures, locations, and ordered spaces. Its basic idea remains consistent: something is neither at one outer side nor the other, but occupies the central place. The exact force in any verse depends on what is being positioned or described there.

e.t: Tekoa is a proper name, functioning as a name rather than a descriptive word. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it identifies a named place or associated locality, appearing seven times across seven verses. Its use is concentrated in historical and prophetic passages, including references in Samuel, Chronicles, Jeremiah, and Amos. Because it is a place-name, its significance comes from the surrounding passage rather than from a broader descriptive meaning. English translations consistently render it as “Tekoa.”

This Hebrew word means “alone,” describing someone or something existing by itself, apart from others. It functions in the Old Testament as a word of separation or isolation rather than as a name or object. It occurs four times in the Hebrew Old Testament, appearing in Leviticus, Psalms, Isaiah, and Hosea. Its repeated rendering as “alone” supports this central meaning across different passages, while the surrounding words determine whether the separation is literal, social, or figurative.
